key_points.point: The document proposes a 'detect-then-mitigate' strategy using CLAP to improve LLM reliability, focusing on procedural detection of hallucinations rather than content-level truth adjudication. By using an attention mechanism over the residual stream, the method identifies hallucinated responses as a procedural failure of the model's internal state. This approach aligns with accelerationist goals by providing a scalable, technical solution to reliability concerns that avoids restrictive, content-based censorship. The document notes that this method is agnostic to the specific LLM architecture, supporting broad deployment.
key_points.verbatim: This allows us to propose a detect-then-mitigate strategy using CLAP to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM reliability compared to direct mitigation approaches.

key_points.point: The document asserts that the residual stream of transformer models contains discriminative information about hallucination that can be extracted via cross-layer attention. By treating layer activations as a sequence, the model can learn to attend to specific layers that are most relevant for detecting factual errors. This belief supports the accelerationist view that model internals are inspectable and that performance can be improved through better architectural utilization rather than just scaling data. The document acknowledges that the specific role of each layer remains a subject for future investigation.
key_points.verbatim: We hypothesise that the contribution of activations at different layers to hallucination detection varies for different tasks. To extract the most relevant information across layers, our method constructs a sequence of tokens by considering the activations at each LLM layer as an input token, and employs an attention mechanism over the sequence input.

key_points.point: The document advocates for using the full residual stream of an LLM to detect hallucinations, arguing that individual layer probes are insufficient for comprehensive behavior monitoring. By processing activations across all layers, the proposed CLAP method aims to provide a more robust oversight mechanism for model outputs. This aligns with safetyist goals of increasing transparency into model decision-making processes to prevent the spread of misinformation. The document notes that this method is particularly effective for fine-grained detection among sampled responses.
key_points.verbatim: While prior work on activation probing has focused on individual layers, in this work we introduce Cross-Layer Attention Probing (CLAP), a fundamentally different approach that utilises the full residual stream (i.e. activations from all LLM layers) to probe model behaviour more comprehensively.

key_points.point: The document demonstrates that CLAP maintains high reliability even when applied out-of-distribution, addressing the safety concern that models often fail when deployed in novel environments. By attending to different layers, the probe generalizes better than single-layer methods, which are prone to domain-specific performance degradation. This is critical for safety, as it ensures that hallucination detection remains functional even when the model encounters data outside its training distribution. The document acknowledges that while CLAP improves generalizability, it is still tested on a limited set of tasks.
key_points.verbatim: Finally, we show that CLAP maintains high reliability even when applied out-of-distribution.

key_points.point: The document highlights the 'jagged' nature of LLM performance, noting that even within the same prompt, sampled responses can vary significantly in factual accuracy. This variability necessitates fine-grained detection methods like CLAP to distinguish between hallucinated and non-hallucinated outputs. From a skeptic perspective, this confirms that LLMs do not possess a stable, coherent understanding of facts, but rather generate probabilistic outputs that require constant external validation. The document notes that this variability is a primary driver of the need for better detection tools.
key_points.verbatim: Next, we build on the observation that different responses sampled for a given prompt can vary, with some being hallucinated and others not.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges the limitations of existing uncertainty estimation methods, which rely on output probabilities and often fail to identify hallucinations in long sequences. By proposing an activation-based probe, the authors aim to move beyond these 'naive' approaches to provide more reliable detection. This aligns with the skeptic view that current LLM evaluation metrics are insufficient and that we need more rigorous, internal-state-based auditing to understand model behavior. The document notes that these methods are necessary because black-box prompting is often restricted to larger, more expensive models.
key_points.verbatim: Overall, current uncertainty estimates, by relying purely on the output probabilities, remain naive approaches to hallucination detection.

factual_claims.claim: CLAP improves hallucination detection performance by up to 1.5% on TQA with Alpaca-7B and Gemma-2B compared to baselines.
CLAP with 128 projection dimension and 2 encoder layers has only 15K parameters for a 2B parameter LLM.
